title: Transactions: correctness under concurrency
lead: A transaction groups several data operations into one unit of work. ACID describes the guarantees on which an application can rely.
goals: Construct a precedence graph from a read/write schedule
Distinguish conflict serializability from view serializability

sections.title: The conceptual map
sections.html:
Moving 5 boxes from the North warehouse to the South warehouse requires two writes: subtracting from North and adding to South. We group these operations into a transaction so that the application does not have to accept a transfer completed only halfway.

  • Atomicity: commit all changes, or abort and remove their effects.
  • Consistency: a transaction must preserve invariants, such as an unchanged total number of boxes. The application still has to implement its business rules correctly.
  • Isolation: in the serializability model studied here, transactions may interleave, but their effects must be equivalent to some serial execution order.
  • Durability: committed results survive the kinds of failures that the system promises to handle.

The DBMS manages database reads and writes. Shipping a physical item does not automatically reverse when ROLLBACK occurs. Identify the transaction boundary before choosing a mechanism.

Transaction boundaries and implementation families

A database transaction begins, performs reads and writes, then commits or aborts. Schedules abstract these database-object accesses and omit local calculations. They do not include every external action performed by application code. A courier booking or physical shipment cannot be recalled merely by undoing database pages.

Concurrency control can use pessimistic waiting/locking or optimistic validation; atomicity and durability can use logging/recovery or other techniques such as shadowing. These families solve related but distinct problems. A serializability proof does not by itself establish crash durability, and a durable log does not prove that an application's invariant was correctly implemented.

A database aborts after an application requested a physical delivery. Must the delivery be cancelled?

Worked answer. No. Database rollback concerns the recorded database changes. The application needs an explicit protocol for the external action.

Must a database rollback automatically cancel a requested physical delivery?

Worked answer. No. Rollback restores database changes within the transaction boundary. The application needs a separate coordination or compensation protocol for an external action.

sections.title: Worked example: two warehouses
sections.html:
North has 40 boxes and South has 60. T1 moves 5 boxes from North → South, while T2 checks the total. In either serial schedule, with T1 completing before T2 or the reverse, T2 sees 100. If T2 reads North after the subtraction and South before the addition, it instead sees 35 + 60 = 95.

  1. Before the transfer, the quantities are (40,60).
  2. T1 writes North = 35.
  3. T2 reads North = 35 and South = 60.
  4. T1 writes South = 65.

The final database state is correct, but the answer already returned is wrong. Checking only the final state is insufficient; the values read during execution also matter.

Does the final total returning to 100 make the earlier answer 95 correct?

Worked answer. No. T2 combined the quantity after subtraction with the quantity before addition. The returned observation remains inconsistent with either serial order, even though T1 later repairs the final state.

sections.title: Build a conflict graph
sections.html:
A schedule lists database reads and writes in execution order while preserving each transaction’s own operation order. R1(X) means T1 reads object X; W2(Y) means T2 writes object Y. Reads by different transactions can coexist. A write must be ordered relative to another transaction’s read or write of the same object. Such a pair is a conflict. Read the small schedule R1(X), W1(X), R2(X), W2(Y), R1(Y) from left to right.

A graph edge T1 → T2 records the constraint “T1 must come before T2 in an equivalent serial order.” Create that edge for operations from different transactions on the same object when at least one is a write and T1’s operation occurs first.

  1. Create one vertex for each transaction: T1 and T2.
  2. On X, W1 precedes R2, so add T1 → T2.
  3. On Y, W2 precedes R1, so add T2 → T1.
  4. The two edges form a cycle: no serial order can place T1 both before and after T2.

This structure is called a conflict graph or precedence graph. Two reads add no edge, and neither do accesses to different objects.

Key takeaway

A cycle rules out conflict serializability. Each edge imposes an order between two transactions, and a cycle makes those ordering requirements contradictory.

If the final pair becomes R1(Y), W2(Y), every edge points T1 → T2, matching the serial order T1 then T2. Two reads do not create an edge, and neither do operations on different objects.

Check your understanding: Would adding R3(Z) at the start create a cycle? No, because its access to Z conflicts with no other operation.

Conflict-preserving swaps and a three-transaction graph

A schedule retains each transaction's internal operation order. Adjacent operations of different transactions may be swapped without changing conflict order only when they do not conflict: different objects, or two reads of the same object. In R1(A), R2(B), W1(A), W2(B), swapping the adjacent R2(B) and W1(A) is permitted. Swapping conflicting accesses is not justified by the same rule.

Original trace R2(A), W2(A), R1(A), R1(B), W1(B), R3(B), W3(B) yields T2→T1 on A and T1→T3 on B. There is no direct T2/T3 conflict, and the graph is acyclic. To obey every edge, put T2 before T1 and T1 before T3: the serial order is T2,T1,T3. An ordering that obeys every directed edge is called a topological order. Read-read pairs add no edge.

A final state alone is insufficient to test a schedule. Conflict equivalence preserves the ordering of every conflicting pair, so reads and subsequent decisions receive the intended ordering constraints.

For R1(A), W2(A), W1(B), R2(B), and independent R3(C), where can T3 occur in a serial order?

Worked answer. The conflicts require T1 before T2. Independent T3 can be before both, between them, or after both: (T3,T1,T2), (T1,T3,T2), (T1,T2,T3).

For R1(A), W2(A), W1(B), R2(B), and independent R3(C), where can T3 occur?

Worked answer. Both conflicting pairs require T1 before T2. T3 has no ordering edge, so valid orders include (T3,T1,T2), (T1,T3,T2), and (T1,T2,T3). Starting earlier does not itself fix a serial position.

sections.title: Recognize three anomalies
sections.html:
The initial price is 100. T1 writes a price of 80 but has not committed. T2 then reads 80. This is already a dirty read, because T2 has read an uncommitted value written by another transaction.

Key takeaway

A dirty read is identified at the moment of the read. If T1 later commits, the earlier read is still dirty. If T1 aborts, the price returns to 100, but T2 may already have used 80 in its calculation.

  • Unrepeatable read: a transaction reads the same price twice and sees different values because another transaction updates and commits between the reads.
  • Dirty read: a transaction reads another transaction's uncommitted value, regardless of whether the writer eventually commits or aborts.
  • Lost update: two transactions update from the same old value, and a later write overwrites the effect of an earlier update.

Exercise: 8 seats remain. Two customers both read 8 and each writes 7. Two successful bookings should leave 6 seats; a result of 7 is a lost update. Use the schedule R1(Seats), R2(Seats), W1(Seats), W2(Seats). Draw the R–W edges to find the cycle.

Show every conflicting-pair edge

Worked answer. R1 precedes W2 on Seats, giving T1→T2. R2 precedes W1 gives T2→T1. W1 precedes W2 adds T1→T2 again. The read/read pair adds no edge. Both directions remain, so the graph is cyclic and the schedule is not conflict-serializable. The missing decrement is visible in the 7-seat result.

Recoverability is different from serializability

This supplementary bridge asks what happens if the writer aborts. A reader that has used another transaction's uncommitted write may also need to abort; this is cascading-abort risk. In the schedules below, C1 means commit(T1), C2 means commit(T2), and A1 means abort(T1). A1 is an abort event, not data object A.

Compare the same writer T1 and reader T2:

  1. W1(A), R2(A), C2, A1: T2 commits based on work T1 later aborts. This is not recoverable.
  2. W1(A), R2(A), C1, C2: T2 still makes a dirty read, but waits to commit until T1 commits. The schedule is recoverable: the reader commits only after the transaction it read from.
  3. W1(A), C1, R2(A), C2: T2 waits to read until T1 commits. This is cascadeless: it reads only committed writes.

A dirty write overwrites another transaction’s uncommitted write. A strict schedule prevents both dirty reads and dirty writes. Thus strict implies cascadeless, which implies recoverable. These commit/abort dependencies answer a different question from whether the precedence graph is acyclic.

In W1(A), W2(A), C2, C1, there are no reads, so the read-only condition for cascadelessness is vacuously satisfied; nevertheless W2 overwrites an uncommitted write, so the schedule is not strict. Avoid using “cascadeless” as a synonym for “no dirty write.”

Can a dirty read still occur in a recoverable schedule?

Worked answer. Yes. W1(A), R2(A), C1, C2 reads before T1 commits, but the dependent reader commits after T1. Recoverability does not prevent the cascading-abort risk before that commit.

Can a recoverable schedule still contain a dirty read?

Worked answer. Yes. W1(A), R2(A), C1, C2 reads before the writer commits, but the dependent reader commits afterward. Recoverability constrains commit order; it does not eliminate the earlier cascading-abort risk.

sections.title: View equivalence and its limits
sections.html:
View equivalence preserves the source of every read: whether it reads an initial value or a value written by a particular transaction. It also preserves the final writer of each object. A blind write writes an object without first reading that object in the transaction. Consider W1(X), W2(X), W1(X). Its graph has edges in both directions, but it has no reads and T1 is the final writer. It is view-equivalent to T2 followed by T1.

Key takeaway

An acyclic graph characterizes conflict serializability. A cycle alone does not disprove view serializability: the blind-write example here still preserves every read source and final writer.

This example explains why conflict serializability is the stricter condition. A cyclic schedule does not necessarily fail every definition of equivalence; the precise conclusion is that it fails the conflict criterion. Real applications also need abort handling and durability, beyond the graph test.

Track read sources as well as final writers

View equivalence preserves initial-value reads, reads-from relationships and the final writer for each object. Original trace R1(A), W2(A), W1(A), W3(A) has a conflict cycle T1↔T2, but R1 reads the initial value and T3 is the final writer. The serial order T1,T2,T3 preserves those view conditions, so this trace is view-serializable despite failing conflict serializability.

By contrast, in R1(A), W2(A), R1(A), T1 first reads the initial value and then reads T2's value. Placing all of T1 before T2 loses the second read source; placing it after T2 loses the initial read. No serial order preserves both. Blind writes explain why a conflict cycle alone is insufficient to reject every form of view equivalence.

Why does the first trace preserve its view in serial order T1,T2,T3?

Worked answer. T1 still reads A before any transaction writes it, and T3 remains A's final writer. T2's and T1's intermediate blind writes have no dependent reads.

Why does T1,T2,T3 preserve the view of R1(A), W2(A), W1(A), W3(A)?

Worked answer. T1 still reads the initial value and T3 remains the final writer. No read depends on an intermediate blind write by T1 or T2, so those view conditions survive even though some write/write conflict order changes.

quiz.question: Is R1(A), W2(A), W1(B), R2(B) conflict-serializable?
options: Yes, in the order T1 then T2
Yes, in the order T2 then T1
No, because the graph has a cycle
There is insufficient information because two objects are involved
quiz.explanation: Both R1(A) before W2(A) and W1(B) before R2(B) create T1 → T2. There is no edge in the reverse direction.

source.summary: Lecture 19 introduces transactions, ACID, execution schedules, conflicts, and two serializability criteria. A dependency graph checks conflict serializability, while logging or shadow paging supports atomicity and durability.
